# 1. Overview

This report demonstrates a reproducible pipeline for cleaning clinical data
before statistical analysis. Using the **Pima Indians Diabetes** dataset,
I show how to:

1. Inspect raw data for structural problems
2. Identify **biologically impossible values** that are actually disguised missing data
3. Visualize missingness patterns
4. Compare two missing-data strategies (complete-case vs median imputation)
5. Produce a publication-ready **Table 1** and a **300 dpi figure**

**Why this matters:** most real-world clinical datasets contain coded missing
values (zeros, 999, -1) that silently corrupt analyses if not detected. This
pipeline catches them and documents every decision.

---

# 2. Setup

```{r libraries}
library(tidyverse)   # data manipulation and plotting
library(janitor)     # cleaning helpers
library(skimr)       # rich descriptive summaries
library(naniar)      # missing-data visualization
library(gtsummary)   # publication-ready tables
library(here)        # reproducible file paths
```

```{r paths}
# Define directories relative to project root
dir_raw     <- here("data", "raw")
dir_cleaned <- here("data", "cleaned")
dir_figures <- here("figures")
dir_output  <- here("output")

# Create output directories if they don't exist
walk(c(dir_cleaned, dir_figures, dir_output),
     ~ dir.create(.x, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE))
```

---

# 3. Load the raw data

The dataset contains `r 768` observations of `r 8` clinical predictors plus a
binary outcome (`Outcome`: 1 = diabetes, 0 = no diabetes).

```{r load-data}
# Define the URL and the destination file path
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jbrownlee/Datasets/master/pima-indians-diabetes.data.csv"
dest_file <- here("data", "raw", "pima_diabetes.csv")

# Download the file if it doesn't already exist
if (!file.exists(dest_file)) {
  download.file(url, dest_file, mode = "wb")
}

# Load the data to verify it's the correct version
diabetes_raw <- read_csv(dest_file, col_names = FALSE)

# Check for the impossible zeros (the values should match these)
# Note: This CSV does not have column headers, so we use column positions.
sum(diabetes_raw$X2 == 0) # Glucose: should be 5
sum(diabetes_raw$X6 == 0) # BMI: should be 11
sum(diabetes_raw$X5 == 0) # Insulin: should be 374
```

```{r rename-variables}
# Add the original column names
colnames(diabetes_raw) <- c(
  "Pregnancies",
  "Glucose",
  "BloodPressure",
  "SkinThickness",
  "Insulin",
  "BMI",
  "DiabetesPedigreeFunction",
  "Age",
  "Outcome"
)
```

```{r glimpse}
glimpse(diabetes_raw)
```

We have `r nrow(diabetes_raw)` rows and `r ncol(diabetes_raw)` columns, all
numeric or integer. No `NA` values are visible yet — which is exactly the trap
we investigate next.

---

# 4. First inspection

```{r skim}
skim(diabetes_raw)
```

**What to notice:**

- `Insulin` and `SkinThickness` have very wide ranges and suspicious lows.
- Several variables have a **minimum of 0**. In a living human, glucose, blood
  pressure, BMI, insulin, and skin thickness cannot be zero. These zeros are
  **impossible values**, and in this dataset they function as missing-data codes.

---

# 5. Identify impossible zeros

The following variables cannot biologically be zero:

| Variable | Meaning | Zero is impossible because |
|---|---|---|
| Glucose | Plasma glucose (mg/dL) | Fatal at 0 |
| BloodPressure | Diastolic BP (mm Hg) | Fatal at 0 |
| SkinThickness | Triceps skinfold (mm) | Not physically possible |
| Insulin | Serum insulin (mu U/mL) | Not compatible with life |
| BMI | Body mass index | Not physically possible |

```{r count-zeros}
vars_with_impossible_zeros <- c(
  "Glucose", "BloodPressure", "SkinThickness", "Insulin", "BMI"
)

zero_summary <- diabetes_raw %>%
  summarise(across(all_of(vars_with_impossible_zeros),
                   ~ sum(.x == 0, na.rm = TRUE))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(),
               names_to  = "variable",
               values_to = "n_zeros") %>%
  mutate(pct_zeros = round(100 * n_zeros / nrow(diabetes_raw), 1))

zero_summary
```

`Insulin` is the worst offender — `r zero_summary %>% filter(variable == "Insulin") %>% pull(pct_zeros)`% of its values are zeros. `SkinThickness` follows at
`r zero_summary %>% filter(variable == "SkinThickness") %>% pull(pct_zeros)`%.

We now recode these zeros to `NA` so R treats them as genuinely missing.

---

# 6. Recode impossible zeros to NA

```{r recode-zeros}
diabetes_clean <- diabetes_raw %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(vars_with_impossible_zeros),
                ~ na_if(.x, 0)))
```

```{r verify-recoding}
diabetes_clean %>%
  summarise(across(all_of(vars_with_impossible_zeros),
                   ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(),
               names_to  = "variable",
               values_to = "n_missing")
```

The missing counts now match the zero counts from Section 5, confirming the
recode worked.

---

# 7. Visualize missingness

```{r miss-var, fig.height=5}
gg_miss_var(diabetes_clean) +
  labs(title = "Missing values by variable",
       subtitle = "After recoding biologically impossible zeros",
       x = "Number of missing values",
       y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

```{r miss-upset, fig.height=5}
gg_miss_upset(diabetes_clean,
              nsets = length(vars_with_impossible_zeros))
```

**Reading the upset plot:** the bars show how many rows are missing in each
*combination* of variables. Most rows are complete; a minority are missing
only `Insulin`, only `SkinThickness`, or both.

---

# 8. Handle missing data — two strategies

There is no universally correct answer. What matters is that the choice is
**documented and defensible**. I compare two standard approaches.

## 8.1 Complete-case analysis

Rows with any missing value are removed.

```{r complete-cases}
diabetes_complete <- diabetes_clean %>%
  drop_na()

n_complete <- nrow(diabetes_complete)
n_raw      <- nrow(diabetes_clean)
```

This retains **`r n_complete`** of `r n_raw` rows
(`r round(100 * n_complete / n_raw, 1)`%).

**Pros:** Simple, no assumptions, unbiased if data are MCAR.
**Cons:** Loses `r n_raw - n_complete` rows, reduces statistical power.

## 8.2 Median imputation

Missing values are replaced with the column median.

```{r median-imputation}
diabetes_imputed <- diabetes_clean %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(vars_with_impossible_zeros),
                ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), median(.x, na.rm = TRUE), .x)))
```

**Pros:** Retains all rows.
**Cons:** Shrinks variance, distorts distributions, underestimates uncertainty.

**Recommendation for this dataset:** complete-case analysis, because
`Insulin` is missing in nearly half the rows and imputing it would create
more bias than it removes. In a real project I would discuss this with the
client and consider multiple imputation (`mice`) if the missingness were
more moderate.

# 9. Descriptive statistics

```{r descriptives}
diabetes_complete %>%
  select(-Outcome) %>%
  skim() %>%
  print()
```

---

# 10. Table 1 — characteristics by outcome

```{r table1}
table1 <- diabetes_complete %>%
  mutate(Outcome = factor(Outcome,
                          levels = c(0, 1),
                          labels = c("No Diabetes", "Diabetes"))) %>%
  tbl_summary(
    by = Outcome,
    statistic = list(
      all_continuous()  ~ "{median} ({p25}, {p75})",
      all_categorical() ~ "{n} ({p}%)"
    ),
    digits = all_continuous() ~ 1,
    label = list(
      Pregnancies              ~ "Number of pregnancies",
      Glucose                  ~ "Plasma glucose (mg/dL)",
      BloodPressure            ~ "Diastolic blood pressure (mm Hg)",
      SkinThickness            ~ "Triceps skinfold (mm)",
      Insulin                  ~ "Serum insulin (mu U/mL)",
      BMI                      ~ "Body mass index",
      DiabetesPedigreeFunction ~ "Diabetes pedigree function",
      Age                      ~ "Age (years)"
    )
  ) %>%
  add_p() %>%
  add_n() %>%
  bold_labels() %>%
  modify_header(label = "**Characteristic**")

table1
```

```{r save-table1, include=FALSE}
table1 %>%
  as_gt() %>%
  gt::gtsave(filename = file.path(dir_output, "table1_by_outcome.html"))
```

**Interpretation:** the diabetes group has notably higher median glucose,
BMI, and age. Formal testing is deferred to the analysis stage — this report
is about *cleaning*, not inference.

---

# 11. Publication-ready figure

```{r figure-glucose, fig.height=5.5}
fig_glucose <- diabetes_complete %>%
  mutate(Outcome = factor(Outcome,
                          levels = c(0, 1),
                          labels = c("No Diabetes", "Diabetes"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Outcome, y = Glucose, fill = Outcome)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.75, outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.25, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#4C72B0", "#C44E52")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Plasma glucose by diabetes status",
    subtitle = paste0("Pima Indians Diabetes dataset (n = ",
                      n_complete, " complete cases)"),
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Plasma glucose (mg/dL)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

fig_glucose
```

```{r save-figure, include=FALSE}
ggsave(file.path(dir_figures, "glucose_by_outcome.png"),
       fig_glucose, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300)
ggsave(file.path(dir_figures, "glucose_by_outcome.pdf"),
       fig_glucose, width = 7, height = 5)
```

Both PNG (300 dpi) and PDF versions are saved — journals typically require one
or the other.

---

# 12. Save the cleaned dataset

```{r save-cleaned}
write_csv(diabetes_complete,
          file.path(dir_cleaned, "diabetes_complete.csv"))

write_csv(diabetes_imputed,
          file.path(dir_cleaned, "diabetes_imputed.csv"))
```

---

# 13. Summary of decisions

| Decision | Choice | Justification |
|---|---|---|
| Impossible zeros | Recoded to `NA` | Zeros are biologically impossible; treat as missing |
| Missing-data strategy | Complete-case | Insulin missing in ~49% of rows; imputation would bias results |
| Final sample size | `r n_complete` rows | Retains sufficient power for downstream modelling |
| Figure format | PNG 300 dpi + PDF | Meets journal submission requirements |
